title: Throwing Up Bile After Drinking: Yellow, Green, and When to Worry
excerpt: Throwing up yellow or green bile after drinking usually means your stomach is empty. What bile is, why alcohol makes you vomit it, what the colors mean, how to settle your stomach, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Throwing up yellow or green bile after drinking? Why it happens, what the colors mean, how to settle your stomach, and the signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** throwing up yellow or green liquid after drinking is almost always bile, and in a social drinker it usually just means your stomach is empty. After you've vomited up the food and drink, your body can keep retching, and that squeezing pulls bile up from the small intestine into your stomach and out. It tastes bitter and looks alarming, but on its own it's a sign of an empty stomach and an irritated gut, not of liver damage. What matters more is what comes with it: whether you can keep fluids down, whether there's blood, and whether the person vomiting is fully awake. This guide explains what bile is, why alcohol makes you bring it up, what the different colors mean, how to settle your stomach, and when to get help.

**The quick rules:** Stop drinking. After the last time you vomit, wait about 15 to 30 minutes, then take small sips of water or an oral rehydration drink every few minutes. Move to plain food like crackers or toast once sips stay down. Skip ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen while your stomach is raw. And never leave someone who is very drunk and vomiting alone or lying on their back.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 right away if** someone who has been drinking is vomiting while confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, has slow or irregular breathing, has cold, clammy, or bluish skin, or has a seizure. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and vomiting while not fully conscious can cause choking. **Go to an emergency room if** you vomit bright red blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, have severe belly pain or pain that spreads to your back, have sudden severe chest pain after retching, can't keep down even small sips of water for more than about 12 hours, or show signs of serious dehydration (very little or no urine, dizziness when you stand, a racing heart). **See a doctor within a day or two if** the vomiting keeps coming back after you drink, you vomit bile on days you haven't been drinking, or it comes with yellow skin or eyes or dark urine. If you drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, sick, or anxious when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor rather than handling it alone.

## What Is Bile, and Why Is It in My Vomit?

Bile is a yellow-green digestive fluid made by your liver and stored in your gallbladder, a small pouch tucked under the liver. When you eat, especially fatty food, the gallbladder squeezes bile into the first part of your small intestine (the duodenum), just past the stomach. There it helps break down fats so you can absorb them. Its color comes mostly from bilirubin, a pigment left over when your body recycles old red blood cells.

Bile isn't supposed to be in your stomach. A ring of muscle at the bottom of the stomach, the pyloric valve, mostly keeps the stomach's contents moving one way, down into the intestine. But vomiting is a forceful, whole-body event. Your diaphragm and belly muscles clamp down hard, and the normal one-way flow can reverse. When your stomach is full, you bring up whatever you ate and drank. Once it's empty and you keep heaving, the squeezing can draw fluid backward from the duodenum into the stomach, and that fluid contains bile.

That's why bile tends to show up late in a bout of vomiting, or the morning after, rather than at the start. It's the "there's nothing left in there" stage. It's also why the vomit tastes so bitter and burns: bile is bitter, and the stomach acid it comes up with stings your throat.

## Why Does Alcohol Make You Throw Up in the First Place?

Vomiting after drinking isn't one problem. Several things happen at once, and they add up.

### 1. Alcohol irritates your stomach lining

Alcohol, especially in stronger drinks, irritates the protective lining of the stomach and causes short-term inflammation that doctors call acute gastritis. It also increases acid production. An irritated, acidic stomach is primed to reject what's in it. If your stomach also hurts, our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) covers that side of things in more detail.

### 2. Acetaldehyde builds up

Your liver breaks alcohol down in two steps. The first step turns alcohol into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound that causes nausea, flushing, and a fast heartbeat. The second step clears acetaldehyde into a harmless substance. When you drink faster than your liver can keep up, acetaldehyde accumulates, and nausea and vomiting are among the first signs. People whose bodies clear acetaldehyde slowly, including many people of East Asian descent, often feel sick after fewer drinks.

### 3. Your brain's vomiting center gets the signal

A small area at the base of the brain, the chemoreceptor trigger zone, monitors your blood for toxins. It sits partly outside the barrier that protects the rest of the brain, so it can "taste" what's circulating. High levels of alcohol and acetaldehyde set it off, and it tells your body to empty the stomach. In a sense, vomiting after heavy drinking is your body trying to stop more alcohol from being absorbed.

### 4. Your stomach empties more slowly

Alcohol can slow how quickly the stomach passes its contents into the intestine. Food and drink sit there longer, which adds to the bloated, queasy feeling.

### 5. Low blood sugar, dehydration, and poor sleep

Alcohol makes you pee more, so you lose fluid. It can also push blood sugar down, especially if you drank without eating, and it wrecks sleep quality. All of these make nausea worse the next morning, which is often when the bile-vomiting happens.

## Throwing Up Yellow Bile After Drinking

Yellow vomit after drinking is the most common version. It usually means one of two things:

- **Your stomach is empty and you're bringing up bile.** This is typical if you've already vomited several times, or if you went to bed without eating and wake up retching.
- **It's just the color of what you drank.** Beer, some ciders, orange juice mixers, and yellow or orange cocktails can all make vomit look yellow. If it's thin and smells like the drink, that's probably it.

Bile on its own tends to be bright or mustard yellow, sometimes foamy, and noticeably bitter. Seeing it once or twice the morning after a big night is expected and usually settles once your stomach has calmed down and you've started rehydrating. It's a sign to stop, rest, and focus on fluids, not a sign that something is wrong with your liver.

## Throwing Up Green Bile After Drinking

Green vomit can look more frightening than yellow, but in the drinking context it's usually the same thing. Bile is naturally yellow-green, and it can look greener depending on how concentrated it is and how long it has been sitting in your stomach. Green food coloring, mint or melon liqueurs, and green mixers can also tint vomit.

Where green vomit becomes more concerning is when it **isn't** explained by drinking or an empty stomach. Repeated green vomiting together with a swollen, painful belly and an inability to pass stool or gas can be a sign of a bowel blockage, which needs emergency care. That picture is quite different from a hangover: it doesn't ease as the hours pass, and the belly pain and bloating are the main feature. If that sounds like you, get seen the same day.

Dark green or brown vomit that smells like stool is also an emergency sign of a blockage and needs immediate care.

## Throwing Up Clear Liquid After Drinking

Clear or whitish vomit after drinking is usually water, saliva, and stomach secretions. It's what comes up when you've already emptied your stomach and then drunk water, or when you vomit early in the morning before eating. It can also look foamy, because swallowed saliva and air mix with the fluid.

Clear vomit on its own isn't a warning sign. The thing to watch is whether you can keep anything down. If you're sipping water and it comes straight back up every time, slow down: wait a bit longer, then try smaller sips (a tablespoon or so) or ice chips. If you still can't keep any fluid down after many hours, you can become dehydrated quickly, and that's a reason to get medical help.

## Dry Heaving After Drinking

Dry heaving is retching with little or nothing coming up. It often follows the bile stage: your stomach is empty, but the vomiting reflex is still firing. It's exhausting, it can make your ribs and belly ache, and it's the moment when people are most likely to strain hard.

A few things help:

- **Breathe slowly through your nose.** Slow, deep breaths can ease the urge.
- **Sit upright or lie on your side,** not flat on your back.
- **Take tiny sips** once the heaving eases, rather than gulping. A big swallow of water on an empty, irritated stomach often triggers another round.
- **Cool air and a cool cloth** on the back of your neck can help some people.

Very forceful or prolonged retching can occasionally cause a small tear in the lining where the food pipe meets the stomach (a Mallory-Weiss tear). The sign is streaks of red blood in vomit after hard heaving. Many of these heal on their own, but any blood in vomit should be checked by a doctor. Much more rarely, violent retching can rupture the food pipe, which causes sudden, severe chest or upper-belly pain and is a surgical emergency.

## What the Color and Texture of Your Vomit Can Tell You

This is a rough guide, not a diagnosis. Context matters more than color: what you drank, whether you ate, and how you feel overall.

| What you see | What it usually means after drinking | When it's a concern |
|---|---|---|
| Yellow, bitter | Bile from an empty stomach, or a yellow drink | Repeated for more than a day, or with yellow skin or eyes |
| Green | Bile, or a green drink or food | With a swollen belly and no stool or gas, or smelling like stool |
| Clear or foamy white | Water, saliva, stomach fluid | When nothing stays down for many hours |
| Red or pink | A red drink (wine, fruit punch) or a small tear from retching | Bright red blood, or more than a few streaks |
| Dark brown "coffee grounds" | Can be old blood | Always: go to an emergency room |
| Food chunks | Stomach not yet empty | Not a concern on its own |

Red wine and red mixers are a common false alarm. If it's the same color as your drink and there's no fresh red streaking, it's probably the drink. If you're not sure, err on the side of getting checked.

## Throwing Up Bile the Morning After Drinking

A lot of people find this page because they woke up and vomited bile, sometimes having not been sick at all the night before. That pattern makes sense. Your stomach has been empty for hours, acetaldehyde and dehydration are peaking, and your blood sugar may be low. The first thing that moves in your stomach, even a sip of water or the smell of coffee, can set off a round of retching, and with nothing else in there, bile is what comes up.

What usually helps:

1. **Rinse your mouth, then rest for 15 to 30 minutes.** Let the reflex settle before you try anything.
2. **Start with tiny sips.** Water, an oral rehydration drink, diluted sports drink, or flat ginger ale. A sip every few minutes beats a full glass at once.
3. **Eat something plain as soon as sips stay down.** Dry crackers, toast, plain rice, a banana, or applesauce. Small amounts. Food helps steady blood sugar and gives the stomach something other than acid and bile to work with.
4. **Try ginger.** Ginger has reasonable evidence for easing nausea in other settings like pregnancy, and it's a low-risk thing to try. See our guide to [ginger for hangovers](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) for what's known.
5. **Avoid coffee, greasy food, and more alcohol** until your stomach has settled. "Hair of the dog" just delays the hangover and adds more acetaldehyde.

Most people find the vomiting has stopped within a few hours and the nausea fades over the rest of the day. For a longer guide to calming the queasy feeling, see our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).

## How to Rehydrate After Vomiting Bile

Vomiting loses water and salts like sodium and potassium on top of the fluid alcohol already pushed out. Plain water is fine, but a drink with some salt and sugar is absorbed better when you've lost a lot of fluid. That's the idea behind oral rehydration solutions, which the World Health Organization has long recommended for dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea.

Practical options:

- **Oral rehydration drinks** such as Pedialyte or similar powders.
- **Sports drinks,** possibly diluted with water if they upset your stomach. They're higher in sugar and lower in sodium than rehydration drinks.
- **Broth or clear soup** once you can manage it, which brings salt and a little warmth.
- **Ice chips or frozen rehydration pops** if even sips come back up.

Our comparison of [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for hangovers](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) goes into which is better for what, and our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains why these salts matter.

Signs you're getting more dehydrated than you can fix at home include very dark urine or none for eight hours or more, dizziness or fainting when you stand, a racing heart at rest, and confusion. Those are reasons to get medical care, where IV fluids can help quickly.

## What About Medicines for Vomiting After Drinking?

Be cautious here, because your stomach is irritated and there may still be alcohol in your system.

- **Ibuprofen, aspirin, and naproxen:** best avoided while you're vomiting. They irritate the stomach lining and raise the risk of bleeding, and alcohol already does both. Their labels carry a stomach-bleeding warning for people who have three or more drinks a day.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol):** easier on the stomach, but it's processed by the liver, and you shouldn't take it while you're still drinking or in large doses. Read our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before reaching for it.
- **Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol):** sometimes used for an upset stomach, but it contains a salicylate related to aspirin, so the same stomach cautions apply. Our [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol) page covers the details.
- **Antacids:** a simple antacid can ease the burning from acid that comes up with bile. If heartburn is the main problem, see our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).
- **Motion-sickness tablets** like dimenhydrinate or meclizine can cause drowsiness, which adds to the sedating effect of any alcohol still in your system. Don't combine them with drinking, and check with a pharmacist first.

Prescription anti-nausea medicines exist, and a doctor can give one if vomiting won't stop. That's one of the reasons it's worth getting seen if you can't keep fluids down.

## Is Throwing Up Bile a Sign of Liver Damage?

Usually not. Bile comes from the liver, so it's natural to worry, but bringing up bile after drinking says more about your stomach being empty than about how your liver is doing. A healthy liver makes bile every day.

Liver trouble from alcohol tends to show up in other ways: yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes (jaundice), dark urine, pale stools, swelling in the belly or legs, easy bruising, and ongoing tiredness or poor appetite. Those signs need a doctor's visit regardless of whether you've vomited. Our [liver health guide](/never-hungover/liver-health-complete-guide-optimal-liver-function-protection-2025) explains what affects the liver over time.

## When Throwing Up Bile Is More Serious

For a social drinker after one big night, bile-vomiting is unpleasant but usually harmless. A few situations are different and deserve plain warnings:

- **Alcohol poisoning.** If someone is vomiting and also confused, very sleepy, hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has cold, pale, or bluish skin, call 911. Don't let them "sleep it off." Roll them onto their side so vomit can drain, stay with them, and don't give them coffee or a cold shower. Our page on [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) walks through what to look for.
- **Pancreatitis.** Severe, steady pain in the upper belly that bores through to your back, often with repeated vomiting, can be inflammation of the pancreas. Heavy drinking is one of its most common causes. It needs urgent care.
- **Blood in vomit.** Bright red blood, clots, or coffee-ground material means bleeding somewhere in the upper gut. Go to an emergency room.
- **Vomiting that won't stop.** If you can't keep down even small sips for more than about 12 hours, or vomiting lasts beyond a day, see a doctor. Prolonged vomiting can upset your body's salt balance in ways that need treatment.
- **Alcoholic ketoacidosis.** In people who drink heavily over days and stop eating, a dangerous buildup of acids in the blood can cause repeated vomiting, belly pain, and fast breathing. It's treatable but needs a hospital.
- **Bile vomiting when you haven't been drinking.** If you regularly bring up bile or have bitter fluid rising into your throat on sober days, that can be bile reflux or another digestive problem, and it's worth raising with a doctor.

If you drink heavily most days and the vomiting starts when you cut back, along with shakes, sweating, or anxiety, that may be withdrawal. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so please talk to a doctor or go to urgent care rather than pushing through on your own.

## How to Avoid Throwing Up Bile Next Time

The single biggest factor is how much alcohol you drink and how fast. Everything else helps a little at the margins. Here's what's worth doing:

- **Eat a real meal before you drink.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which keeps peak levels lower. Drinking on an empty stomach is one of the most reliable routes to vomiting; our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why.
- **Pace yourself.** Your liver clears roughly one standard drink an hour, give or take. Drinking faster than that is what lets acetaldehyde pile up.
- **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace and offsets some of the fluid loss.
- **Watch the strong stuff.** Shots and high-strength cocktails hit your stomach lining harder and raise your blood alcohol faster.
- **Stop at the first wave of nausea.** It's your body's early warning. Switching to water at that point often heads off the vomiting entirely.
- **Have something salty and some water before bed.** Going to sleep with an empty stomach and dry mouth sets up the morning bile round.

For a full rundown of the habits with the best evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

### Where DHM fits in

Some people also take DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or while drinking. Lab and animal research suggests it may help the body process alcohol and acetaldehyde, and it has been studied for effects on how alcohol acts in the brain. Human research is limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents vomiting or stops you from getting sick if you drink too much. It doesn't change the basics above: eating first, pacing, and drinking less do far more. If you'd like to try it as an add-on, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicine, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

Throwing up yellow or green bile after drinking is your body's way of saying the stomach is empty and still irritated. For most social drinkers it passes within a few hours with rest, small sips of fluid, and plain food. The color itself matters less than the company it keeps. Blood or coffee-ground vomit, severe belly or back pain, confusion or drowsiness, and being unable to keep fluids down are the signs that mean you need care, not more time. And if bile-vomiting has become a regular part of your weekends, the most effective fix is the simplest one: eat first, slow down, and drink less.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why am I throwing up bile after drinking?**

Because your stomach is empty. Once you've vomited up the food and drink, continued retching pulls bile up from the small intestine into the stomach. Alcohol drives the vomiting by irritating the stomach lining, raising acetaldehyde levels, and triggering the brain's vomiting center. On its own, bile in your vomit is not a sign of liver damage.

**Is throwing up yellow bile after drinking bad?**

Usually not. Yellow bile after a night of drinking typically means your stomach is empty and still irritated. It should settle within hours as you rest and rehydrate with small sips. It's a concern if it lasts more than a day, if you can't keep any fluids down, or if it comes with blood, severe belly pain, yellow skin or eyes, or confusion.

**What does green vomit mean after drinking?**

In most cases it's bile, which is naturally yellow-green, or the color of a green drink or food. Green vomit is more concerning if it comes with a swollen, painful belly and you can't pass stool or gas, or if it smells like stool. Those can be signs of a bowel blockage and need emergency care.

**Why am I throwing up clear liquid after drinking?**

Clear or foamy vomit is usually water, saliva, and stomach fluid. It's common after your stomach has already emptied, or if you drink water too quickly afterward. Wait 15 to 30 minutes after vomiting, then sip small amounts. If nothing stays down for about 12 hours, get medical help for dehydration.

**How do I stop throwing up bile after drinking?**

Stop drinking, rest for 15 to 30 minutes after the last time you vomit, then take small sips of water or an oral rehydration drink every few minutes. Add plain food like crackers or toast once sips stay down, and try ginger. Avoid ibuprofen, aspirin, coffee, and more alcohol. If vomiting won't stop, a doctor can prescribe anti-nausea medicine.

**How long does vomiting last after drinking?**

For most people, vomiting from a night of drinking stops within a few hours, and the nausea fades over the rest of the day as alcohol and acetaldehyde clear. If vomiting continues beyond about 24 hours, or you can't keep down fluids for 12 hours, see a doctor.

**Should I make myself throw up after drinking?**

No. Making yourself vomit doesn't meaningfully lower your blood alcohol, because alcohol is absorbed quickly once it's in your stomach. Forcing it irritates the stomach and food pipe, adds to dehydration, and can cause choking if you're very drunk. If you feel sick, stop drinking, switch to water, and sit upright.

**When should I go to the ER for vomiting after drinking?**

Call 911 if the person is confused, very drowsy, hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has bluish skin, since these are signs of alcohol poisoning. Go to an emergency room for vomit with blood or coffee-ground material, severe belly or back pain, sudden chest pain after retching, or signs of severe dehydration like no urine, fainting, or a racing heart.
